_note: Week 2 structure is stubbed with sample scenarios to demonstrate the Problem Solver component. Add the remaining scenarios (aim for 10-15 total) as you build out full Week 2 content.

scenarios.title: Concrete Was Poured in Rain; Quality Questionable
scenarios.problem: A concrete pour was completed yesterday afternoon during a rain event you weren't on site for. Quality is now in question.
symptoms: Water pooling visible on the surface in photos
No inspection report on file for the pour
correctActions: Review the daily report and weather log from the pour date
Inspect the cured surface for signs of surface weakness (scaling, dusting)
Consult with the QA/QC manager or structural engineer if defects are suspected
Consider core testing if there's reasonable doubt about strength
scenarios.documentation: Log the concern in the daily report, attach photos, and open an RFI or NCR if testing confirms an issue.
commonMistakes: Assuming it's fine because it "looks okay" on the surface
Not checking whether the pour should have been stopped per the site's weather protocol
Failing to loop in QA/QC before the next phase starts

scenarios.title: Subcontractor Showing Up Late; Schedule Impact
scenarios.problem: The electrical subcontractor has shown up 2+ hours late for the past three days, threatening the rough-in schedule.
symptoms: Downstream trades (drywall) are starting to stack up behind schedule
Foreman gives inconsistent explanations each day
correctActions: Document each late arrival with times in the daily report
Raise it with the Superintendent early — don't wait for it to become a crisis
Ask the sub's foreman directly what's causing it and whether it's a pattern
Recommend a recovery plan if the sub agrees to one (extra crew, weekend work)
scenarios.documentation: Daily report entries with timestamps; a schedule impact note if it starts threatening a milestone.
commonMistakes: Letting it slide because "it's just a couple hours"
Not connecting the dots between recurring lateness and schedule risk until it's a major delay

scenarios.title: Defect Found in Rough-In MEP Before Next Trade Starts
scenarios.problem: You find a plumbing rough-in defect (wrong pipe slope) during your pre-drywall inspection, and drywall is scheduled to start tomorrow.
symptoms: Pipe slope measured out of tolerance during your walk
Drywall crew already mobilized for tomorrow
correctActions: Stop the drywall close-up in that area — do not let it get covered
Notify the plumbing foreman and Superintendent immediately
Get the fix scheduled and re-inspect before authorizing drywall in that specific area
Communicate the delay (if any) to the drywall foreman directly, not just through the Super
scenarios.documentation: Photo + measurement + location + NCR if it's a spec deviation; note the corrective timeline in the daily report.
commonMistakes: Letting drywall proceed to "stay on schedule" and hoping it's caught later
Not re-inspecting after the fix before sign-off

scenarios.title: Change Order Request From Owner; Scope/Budget Impact
scenarios.problem: The Owner's rep requests an on-the-spot layout change that isn't in the current drawings.
symptoms: Verbal request with no formal documentation
Trade foreman asking if they should proceed
correctActions: Do not authorize field trades to proceed on verbal direction alone
Document the request in detail and route it to the PM immediately
Let the PM/Super determine if a formal change order is needed before work proceeds
Keep the trade on hold or on other work until direction is confirmed in writing
scenarios.documentation: Written summary of the request, who made it, and the date; attach to the RFI/change order log once formalized.
commonMistakes: Authorizing work based on a verbal request
Not escalating quickly enough, causing the trade to sit idle
